newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: AUSTRALIA "CAN HANDLE" SATELLITE MOP UP
The emergency response team charged with responding to the possible crash landing of a Russian space probe somewhere in Australia will seek help from the United States, if it runs into trouble.
But Brigadier Alan Hodges, who's in charge of the response team, says that will only happen if the clean up job is beyond the capabilities of the Australians.

The probe, which was intended to head for Mars, remained in the earth's atmosphere after its booster rockets failed to fire. It's carrying 200 grams of plutonium, which Brigadier Hodges says may present a new problem for his team if it leaks.
But he believes the Australians have the expertise to cope. - - - -
INVESTIGATORS HOPE TO ENTER GRETLEY COLLIERY
Investigation teams are this afternoon expected to be able to re-enter the section of the Gretley mine at Wallsend, in Newcastle, where four miners were killed last week.
The miners died on Thursday when the tunnel they were working in collapsed and flooded with water from a nearby dis-used mine site.
District check inspector with the miners' union, Les Yates, says about 360-thousand litres of water is being pumped out of the mine section each hour and pumping should be finished today. - - - -
LOW PAID WAGE OFFER NO LONG TERM SOLUTION
Welfare agencies say the Federal Government's eight-dollar-a-week pay increase for workers on below average earnings won't have much long term impact.
The Brotherhood of St Laurence says the rise is welcome, but more must be done.
It says the rise must be pegged to inflation, and the protection it represents should be guaranteed beyond three years.
Jesuit Social Services says the increase must also be passed on to people receiving welfare benefits, because they inhabit the same socio-economic group as the low paid.
QUESTIONS POSED ON ABORIGINAL FUNDING
A leading Aboriginal community leader says an independent inquiry should be launched into the expenditure of money allocated to the states for Aboriginal programs.
Executive Director of the Kimberley Land Council, Peter Yu, says the money isn't reaching its target, because it's squandered on bureaucratic regimes and agencies supposedly delivering services.
Mr Yu says those responsible for allocating the money should be probed by an independent international body, like the United Nations.
He says such a study should look at the cost effectiveness of agencies involved, and how programs are delivered; and also audit the funding arrangements between the Commonwealth and the states.
POTENTIAL NEW VIRUS VICTIMS TO BE VACCINATED
People who are at risk of contracting the Lyssavirus, which claimed the life of a 39-year old Queensland woman on Friday, are being identified so they can be vaccinated.
The woman contracted the virus, a relative of rabies, from a flying fox.
Queensland's Health Minister, Mike Horan, says people who handle flying foxes are most at risk.
Mr Horan says they should use gloves and overalls when working with the animals, as the virus can be transmitted by a deep puncture wound like a bite or a deep scratch.
LOW PAID "MUST BE PROTECTED"
The Brotherhood of St Laurence says there's a danger, under the deregulated industrial relations regime the Coalition is pursuing, of increasing numbers of people being stuck on very low wages.
Director of Social Action and Research, Sue Jackson, has welcomed the announced wage increase for low paid workers, but says the Federal Government needs to come up with long-term solutions.
Ms Jackson says low paid people must be protected in the new system.
She says a failure to guarantee regular, adequate wage increases would raise the prospect of people being stuck on low wages, which prevent them from attaining a decent standard of living.
LISTING OFFSHORE OIL RIG TO BE STABILISED
A plan of action to handle an oil rig, listing in Gulf St Vincent in South Australia since Saturday morning, is expected to be ready late today.
A diving team will carry out an underwater inspection of the Maersk Victory, at first light.
The rig had to be abandoned when one of its legs struck unstable ground, as it was being positioned about 20-nautical miles off Maslin's Beach.
About 35 workers had to be removed from it.
Chris Rann, speaking for exploration company Canyon Australia, says removal of tonnes of oil and diesel fuel, is expected to get underway today.
